findings.headline: 20 council properties fell out of compliance for their annual gas safety check at Q2 because of access issues, with the Legal team applying for injunctions.
findings.detail: The paper reports 99.58% of council homes had all required gas safety checks, against a 100% annual target. All 20 properties have been passed to the Legal team.
findings.matters: Enforced access and injunction costs against housing stock are a potential Housing Revenue Account cost and liability, and other councils with similar access issues would want to know how this was handled.
findings.figures: 99.58% Q2 cumulative; 100% annual target; 99.80% Q1 2026/27; 100.00% Q2 2025/26; 20 properties
findings.quote: 20 properties have fallen out of compliance for their annual gas safety check due to access issues.

findings.headline: Percentage of council and South Essex Homes spend with local businesses across the LGR footprint at 41.93% at Q2, against a >45% quarterly target, rated red.
findings.detail: The paper gives the breakdown by area: Southend at 36.39%, Rochford at 2.87% and Castle Point at 2.67%. It also reports Greater Essex spend at 60.14%.
findings.matters: Local procurement share is a measure councils set themselves and report to members, and a finance director would look at whether the target is being reached under the procurement approach.
findings.figures: 41.93% Q2 local spend across LGR footprint; >45% quarterly target; 40.06% Q1 2026/27; £35,189,230.86 across 1277 suppliers; 36.39% Southend; 60.14% Greater Essex
findings.quote: Breaking down the percentage of spend across the three areas, Southend was 36.39%

findings.headline: The Local Government Reorganisation programme has ceased, following government directive, with effort moving to the Transformation Programme.
findings.detail: The paper says the LGR programme has ceased as per government directive. Transformation Programme initiatives are rated 82% on track against an annual target of above 80%, with business cases for three priority initiatives due in November.
findings.matters: Other councils planning for reorganisation would want to know how a council stood down its LGR work and where its transformation savings and business cases now sit.
findings.figures: 82% Transformation initiatives rated on track; >80% annual target; 78% Q2 2025/26; 88% Q1 2026/27
findings.quote: The Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) programme has ceased, as per government directive and all efforts will now focus on the Transformation Programme delivery.

findings.headline: Children in care rate at 82.0 per 10,000 under-18s at Q2, against a <75.0 annual target, rated red.
findings.detail: The paper gives monthly rates of 81.5 in July, 82.6 in August and 82 in September, and lists the total children looked after at 325 at the end of Q2.
findings.matters: Looked-after numbers are one of the largest demand-led costs in children's services, so a finance director would compare the rate against their own placement budget assumptions.
findings.figures: 82.0 per 10,000 at Q2; 81.5 July; 82.6 August; 82 September; 80.8 Q1 2026/27; 85.4 Q2 2025/26; <75.0 annual target; 325 children looked after at end of Q2
findings.quote: The rate of children in care per 10,000 is 82 (81.5 in July, 82.6 in August and 82 in September).

findings.headline: Council Tax collected at 52.2% at Q2, meeting the 52.2% quarterly target, with a 97.2% year-end target.
findings.detail: The paper states the team met its halfway target after a good month of collection in September and expects to reach the year-end collection target. The measure is rated green.
findings.matters: Council Tax is a core local income stream, and a finance director would compare the halfway position with their own collection profile.
findings.figures: 52.2% cumulative collected; 52.2% quarterly target; 52.1% Q2 2025/26; 97.2% year-end target
findings.quote: The team has achieved their target at the halfway stage of the year following a good month of collection in September and is on course to achieve the year-end target collection of 97.2%.

findings.headline: Business Rates collected at 55.4% at Q2 against a 55.1% quarterly target, with a 98.3% year-end target.
findings.detail: The paper says the team reduced an initial deficit against the collection profile from the end of April and is on course for the year-end target. The measure is rated green.
findings.matters: Business rates collection is a direct driver of retained income, so a finance director would track whether the recovery against the earlier shortfall holds through to year-end.
findings.figures: 55.4% cumulative collected; 55.1% quarterly target; 55.3% Q2 2025/26; 98.3% year-end target
findings.quote: It represents a considerable success for the team and ensures the team is on course to achieve the year-end target of 98.3%.

findings.headline: Capital programme spend at 30.28% of the approved budget at Q2, against a 22.38% quarterly target and a 70% year-end target.
findings.detail: The paper reports Q2 capital spend above its quarterly profile and states that capital challenge sessions will be held in October to review delivery of the programme. The measure is rated green.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know whether spend is running ahead of profile before year-end, and whether the October challenge sessions will change the 70% outturn assumption.
findings.figures: 30.28% Q2 capital budget spent; 22.38% quarterly target; 70% year-end target
findings.quote: For Qtr.2, the percentage of capital budget spent is 30.28%, above the target of 22.38%. There will be capital challenge sessions in October to review the delivery of the capital programme.

findings.headline: The Council is using available cash balances to defer external borrowing, with investment income forecast £0.400M below budget as a result.
findings.detail: The paper says the approach avoids associated borrowing costs and that a £0.200M improvement is forecast through action to reduce service overspending and strengthen cash balances. The paper also reports an estimated £0.100M pressure on externally managed funds, partly due to the redemption of £6M from the Patrizia property fund.
findings.matters: A council choosing to defer borrowing from its own cash, and accepting lower investment income to do so, is a treasury decision that lenders and peers will read directly.
findings.figures: £0.400M reduction in investment income; £0.200M improvement; £0.100M net pressure on externally managed funds; £6M Patrizia fund redemption
findings.quote: using available funds to defer the need for external borrowing

findings.headline: Capital requests net £29.358M of changes to the capital investment programme, including £8.596M of 2026/27 scheme budgets carried forward into later years.
findings.detail: The paper says the review included removing £0.751M of scheme budgets, adding £2.197M of unbudgeted external funding and transferring £17.668M from the subject-to-viable-business-case section into the main programme. Forecast 2026/27 capital expenditure is £88.667M against a September Cabinet budget of £88.268M.
findings.matters: Carry-forwards and transfers from the subject-to-business-case list show how a council is re-profiling an ambitious programme, which lenders and peers can read as a sign of delivery capacity.
findings.figures: £29.358M net requested changes; £8.596M carried forward; £17.668M transferred from subject to viable business case; £0.751M removed; £2.197M added with external funding; £88.667M forecast 2026/27 capital expenditure; £88.268M 2026/27 budget at September Cabinet
findings.quote: This report is seeking approval for £29.358M of net requested changes to the capital investment programme budgets.

findings.headline: The transformation programme reports more than £4M of financial benefits by 30 September, of which £0.460M is forecast to become recurring base budget savings.
findings.detail: The paper says the £4M includes savings, cost avoidance and reductions in forecast overspends, and that the savings target for 2026/27 is £1.080M including undelivered 2025/26 savings. Work continues to convert wider benefits into recurring savings.
findings.matters: The gap between headline benefits and recurring base savings is a distinction a finance director will want to check in their own transformation reporting.
findings.figures: more than £4M financial benefits; £0.460M recurring base budget savings; £1.080M 2026/27 savings target
findings.quote: By 30 September, the transformation programme was already delivering more than £4M of financial benefits through savings, cost avoidance and reductions in forecast overspends.

findings.headline: Benefits Service contracts with Essex County Council and Thurrock Council are forecast to generate additional gross income of £0.530M in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says the income is secured for 2026/27 and that discussions are continuing on extending the arrangements into future years.
findings.matters: Councils selling back-office benefits administration to neighbouring authorities is a revenue model that finance directors elsewhere may want to compare.
findings.figures: £0.530M additional gross income in 2026/27
findings.quote: The increased volume and scope of this work is forecast to generate additional gross income of approximately (£0.530M) in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Housing Benefit costs for supported accommodation are estimated to add £2.410M of gross pressure in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says the Council can only recover 60% subsidy on rental costs above the fair market rent threshold and cannot claim subsidy for some residents placed in supported accommodation who do not meet DWP vulnerability criteria. Favourable movements of £0.700M are forecast to offset part of the pressure.
findings.matters: A subsidy gap on supported accommodation is a national issue, and a finance director elsewhere can compare the scale of the gross pressure with their own caseload exposure.
findings.figures: £2.410M additional gross pressure; approximately £30M annual Rent Allowances and Rent Rebates; 60% subsidy recovery above threshold; £0.700M favourable impact
findings.quote: The additional gross financial pressure in 2026/27 is currently estimated at £2.410M.

findings.headline: The Housing Revenue Account forecasts a £0.850M overspend at Period 6, mainly from around £1M of additional repairs and maintenance investment.
findings.detail: The paper says the repairs pressure includes increased works on damp, mould and condensation and that an action plan is being developed. A £0.200M benefit from South Essex Homes' share of the Essex pension fund being in surplus partly offsets it.
findings.matters: HRA repairs cost pressures linked to damp and mould are a sector-wide issue, and the paper shows an action plan being developed alongside the forecast.
findings.figures: £0.850M HRA forecast overspend; around £1M additional repairs and maintenance investment; £0.200M pension surplus benefit
findings.quote: The Period 6 forecast for the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) indicates an overspend of £0.850M.

findings.headline: Economic conditions could raise the 2027/28 budget gap by a further £2.5M to an estimated £11.5M, against the £9.0M in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy.
findings.detail: The council's provisional assessment excludes service cost pressures that cannot be permanently mitigated this year. The cumulative MTFS gap to 2030/31 is £28.5M.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing medium-term plans will want to see how fast a single-year gap is widening and whether the cumulative gap is being revised.
findings.figures: £2.5M additional gap; £11.5M estimated 2027/28 gap; £9.0M 2027/28 gap in MTFS; £28.5M cumulative gap to 2030/31
findings.quote: the council estimates that these could increase the budget gap by a further £2.5M to an estimated £11.5M in 2027/28.

findings.headline: The unallocated General Fund Reserve is held at £12M, the highest level the council has held, and the s151 Officer recommends keeping it at that level through to 2030/31.
findings.detail: The paper says the reserve was increased in the 2026/27 budget and that a separate £2.5M Children's and £1.0M Adults social care risk reserve was created. It also states that any drawdown should be replenished given the funding outlook for 2027/28 and 2028/29.
findings.matters: A council that has just closed a £12.0M 2025/26 overspend through reserves and is now holding its general reserve at a record level is a clear signal to other councils and to lenders about how the reserve is being protected.
findings.figures: £12M unallocated General Fund Reserve; £2.5M Children's social care risk reserve; £1.0M Adults social care risk reserve; £12.0M 2025/26 overspend
findings.quote: The s151 Officer recommends maintaining this level through to 2030/31

findings.headline: Care packages for Older People are forecast at a £2.730M overspend, a reduction of £0.760M since Period 4, after targeted use of eligible grants.
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction mainly reflects reprioritised grant funding, following delays to the originally planned programme of work. The underlying pressure continues from rising care costs and lower client contributions of around £1.500M.
findings.matters: The paper shows a reduction driven by grant use rather than by lower care costs, which a finance director would want to see separated from underlying recurring pressure.
findings.figures: £2.730M forecast overspend; £0.760M reduction since Period 4; around £1.500M lower client contributions
findings.quote: Care packages for Older People are forecasting an overspend of £2.730M, a reduction of £0.760M since Period 4.

findings.headline: Residential and high-cost supported accommodation placements for children fall from 65 at the end of March 2026 to 54 at the end of September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper reports that placements rose from 50 in November 2025 to 65 in March 2026, fell to 60 by July 2026 and to 54 by September 2026. It describes these as a significant area of financial risk despite the progress.
findings.matters: A falling count of high-cost placements over six months is the mechanism behind the savings figure, and a finance director elsewhere can compare the trajectory with their own placement numbers.
findings.figures: 54 placements at end September 2026; 60 at end July 2026; 65 at end March 2026; 50 at end November 2025; 7 placements over £0.5M per year; 1 placement over £1M per year
findings.quote: which increased from 50 at the end of November 2025 to 65 at the end of March 2026, before reducing to 60 by the end of July 2026 and further reducing to 54 by the end of September 2026.

findings.headline: Children and SEND forecasts a £7.090M overspend, which the paper says has increased, despite £4.360M of targeted savings on Children in Care placements.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to unavoidable new residential and high-cost supported accommodation placements and a national shortage of foster carers. Placement-related pressures account for approximately 92% of the portfolio's forecast overspend.
findings.matters: Children's placement costs are the largest single pressure in the paper, and a reader can see savings from placement reduction being outweighed by new placements in the same period.
findings.figures: £7.090M forecast overspend; £4.360M targeted savings to date; approximately 92% of the portfolio overspend from placements; £1.440M more savings than at Period 4
findings.quote: Despite the continued delivery of targeted savings, the overall revised forecast overspend has increased to £7.090M.

findings.headline: £5.080M of the £6.050M of new savings and income initiatives in the 2026/27 budget are achieved at Period 6, up from 80% at Period 4, with none rated Red.
findings.detail: The remaining initiatives are rated Amber and the paper says work continues to deliver the outstanding savings or identify alternatives. Unachieved savings are included within the relevant portfolio forecasts.
findings.matters: Delivery rate against a stated savings programme halfway through the year is a direct test of whether budget assumptions are holding, and the paper shows the rate rising.
findings.figures: £5.080M achieved; £6.050M approved initiatives; around 84% achieved; 80% at Period 4; £0.970M remaining
findings.quote: Good progress has been made against these initiatives, with around 84% (£5.080M) already achieved. The remaining initiatives continue to be rated Amber, with none rated Red.

findings.headline: Southend-on-Sea forecasts a General Fund overspend of £11.964M at Period 6, an improvement of £1.327M on the £13.291M reported at Period 4.
findings.detail: The paper reports the overspend as 2.8% of gross expenditure and says the improvement has come despite continued demand and cost pressures in Children's services. Children's and Adult Social Care together account for over 108% of the forecast overspend, with other portfolios partly offsetting it.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how a 2.8% general fund overspend, halfway through the year, is being moved by management action rather than by one-off items.
findings.figures: £11.964M forecast overspend; £13.291M at Period 4; £1.327M improvement; 2.8% of gross expenditure budget; over 108% of the overspend from Children's and Adult Social Care
findings.quote: This represents an improvement of £1.327M on the position reported at July 2026 (Period 4) (£13.291M)

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Better Queensway Housing plans Final
findings.headline: The paper says The Range may be entitled to compensation if the council ends its lease on redevelopment grounds, with compensation based on a multiplier of Rateable Value.
findings.detail: The paper refers to s37(2) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954, under which compensation is based on a multiplier of the Rateable Value linked to time in occupation. No amount is given.
findings.matters: A possible compensation liability with no amount stated is a contingent cost for zone 1 that a finance director would need to price.
findings.figures: none given; compensation is based on a multiplier of Rateable Value linked to time in occupation
findings.quote: If the lease is terminated on such grounds, The Range may be entitled compensation for ending the lease.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Better Queensway Housing plans Final
findings.headline: The lease of The Range's site expires on 24 September 2028, and the paper gives a different date of 28 September 2028 in its consultation section.
findings.detail: Discussions with The Range about the lease are described as in hand. The lease has security of tenure under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954, so the council can end it on redevelopment grounds and may then owe compensation.
findings.matters: A lease with statutory security of tenure and a possible compensation liability affects the timing and cost of delivering zone 1.
findings.figures: lease expiry 24 September 2028 (paragraph 4.4) and 28 September 2028 (paragraph 12.2)
findings.quote: The lease of the site occupied by the Range expires on 24 September 2028

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Better Queensway Housing plans Final
findings.headline: The highway works for Better Queensway are, in the paper's words, substantially advanced.
findings.detail: The highway works approved in July 2024 include removing the Queensway underpass and footbridge and building new roundabout and carriageway arrangements. The paper says these works provide the foundation for the residential phases.
findings.matters: A large part of the infrastructure cost has already been committed, and the partner selection process will state that the highways element has already been delivered.
findings.figures: none given
findings.quote: The highway works are now substantially advanced and provide the foundation for the residential phases of the wider regeneration project.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Better Queensway Housing plans Final
findings.headline: The paper says significant work has been undertaken to narrow the viability gap on development zones 1 and 2, with the aim of a fundable scheme.
findings.detail: Viability was assessed for both zones using early scale and massing work, which is set out in an exempt Part 2 appendix. The paper lists cost reduction, growth potential, faster delivery and grant access as ways to improve viability.
findings.matters: A viability gap that is not yet closed means the scheme is not yet fundable on its current terms, and the council's exposure depends on how it is closed.
findings.figures: none in the public paper; viability figures are in the exempt Part 2 appendix
findings.quote: Significant work has been undertaken to narrow the viability gap, and the aim is to deliver a fundable scheme.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Better Queensway Housing plans Final
findings.headline: This decision does not authorise the appointment of an Investment Partner, which will return to Cabinet separately.
findings.detail: Cabinet approves the Investment Partnership approach and the start of the partner selection process. The paper says the detailed governance, financial commitments and risk allocation will return to Cabinet before the council enters into the partnership.
findings.matters: The financial terms of the partnership, including risk allocation and the council's commitments, are not yet set and will come back to Cabinet for approval.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: this approval does not authorise the appointment of an Investment Partner, this will separately be returned to Cabinet for approval.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Better Queensway Housing plans Final
findings.headline: The paper says resource costs beyond 2027/28 will arise over the life of the project, without quantifying them.
findings.detail: Section 7.6 says investment in project delivery support, external advice and specialism for future years will be required and is likely to be significant over a number of years. No figure is given for those later years.
findings.matters: Recurring project-delivery costs with no stated total are an unquantified future commitment for the council's capital programme.
findings.figures: no figure given for years beyond 2027/28
findings.quote: In future years, there will be resource costs beyond those set out above due to the nature of this long-term regeneration project.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Better Queensway Housing plans Final
findings.headline: The housing workstream needs £1.4m of resource for Q4 2026/27 and 2027/28, with £317k already agreed in the 2027/28 budget.
findings.detail: The £1.4m is split into a programme management office (£221k), specialist external support (£910K), and work stream leads (£292k). The paper says the £317k already agreed for 2027/28 leaves an additional request of £1.1m.
findings.matters: Project-delivery and advisory costs are being funded as a separate, rising cost line ahead of any partner being appointed.
findings.figures: £1.4m total; £221k programme management office; £910K specialist external support; £292k work stream leads; £317k budget already agreed for 2027/28; £1.1m additional
findings.quote: The budget already agreed for 2027/28 is £317k, meaning the total request

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Better Queensway Housing plans Final
findings.headline: Paper says Homes England's £15m Housing Infrastructure Funding grant "will be at risk" if the council does not commit to the housing elements
findings.detail: The paper links the continuation of the housing workstream to the Homes England grant. It also says that failing to meet funding conditions or project milestones could place grant funding at risk and lead to clawback.
findings.matters: Grant conditions tied to milestones create a clawback exposure, which matters to any council relying on external funding for a capital scheme.
findings.figures: £15m Housing Infrastructure Funding grant
findings.quote: Housing Infrastructure Funding grant of £15m that Homes England is providing will be at risk

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Better Queensway Housing plans Final
findings.headline: The estimated total build cost of development zones 1 and 2 is circa £330m, before inflation and before anticipated grant funding and cost reductions.
findings.detail: The paper states the £330m figure excludes inflation, anticipated grant funding and cost reductions, which will be refined as the scheme design evolves. It expects the Investment Partnership route to transfer most of this cost and risk to a partner, subject to the agreed structure.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know the cost base is an unindexed, pre-grant estimate, and that the council's share will depend on a partner structure not yet selected.
findings.figures: circa £330m total build cost, zones 1 and 2, excluding inflation and grant
findings.quote: This figure does not include inflation, or anticipated grant funding available as well as cost reductions

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Better Queensway Housing plans Final
findings.headline: Cabinet is asked to approve a £1.1m capital addition funded by borrowing for Better Queensway in 2026/27 and 2027/28, subject to Full Council approval.
findings.detail: Cabinet is asked to approve the additional resource requirement for the rest of 2026/27 and 2027/28 as a capital addition. The paper says the profile of this addition is still to be determined and that Full Council approval is required.
findings.matters: A new borrowing-funded capital addition, with its profile not yet set, will add to the council's borrowing requirement once Full Council approves it.
findings.figures: £1.1m capital expenditure funded by borrowing (2026/27 remainder and 2027/28)
findings.quote: £1.1m capital expenditure funded by borrowing to be added to the capital investment programme

findings.headline: Southend Care Ltd has agreed a further remodelling of some services, with efficiencies effective from the 2027/28 financial year.
findings.detail: The paper says the remodelling will deliver efficiencies from 2027/28, which is the second year of the company's three-year business plan. The paper does not state the size of the efficiencies.
findings.matters: A council company committing to dated efficiencies in its business plan is a savings measure that other councils running similar companies may track, though no figure is given here.
findings.quote: effective from the 27/28 financial year.

findings.headline: Southend Care Ltd reports that recruitment challenges over the past 12 months caused delays, and that all key posts are now filled.
findings.detail: The paper says the position has now stabilised and the company is at routine recruitment of vacancies. It reports staff turnover of 14.5% for the year, and agency spend of 4.5% of the staffing budget excluding short-term 1-1 arrangements.
findings.matters: Delays from recruitment pressure in a council-owned care provider show how staffing constraints can slow the delivery of a planned service change.
findings.figures: staff turnover 14.5%; agency spend 4.5% of staffing budget
findings.quote: Recruitment has been more challenging in the past 12 months for a range of positions and has caused some delays in the activities of the business.

findings.headline: Southend Care Ltd's five-year forecast shows the company remaining in profit throughout the period, and its 2026/27 budget shows a year-end profit.
findings.detail: The paper states the current five-year forecast keeps the company in profit in every year. The forecast figures are in a Part 2 appendix that is not included in this document.
findings.matters: A forecast of continued profit from a council company is relevant to the council's dependence on the company for income and to any risk assessment of its guarantees or support.
findings.figures: 5-year forecast
findings.quote: the current 5-year forecast shows SCL remaining in profit throughout that period.

findings.headline: Southend Care Ltd reports two service areas, Brook Meadows House and Reablement, showing in deficit.
findings.detail: The paper says Brook Meadows House is performing better than budget in year, with private bed occupancy at 96.3%. Reablement is in deficit because the move to the new locality homecare model has a longer implementation period than planned.
findings.matters: A deficit in a service undergoing remodelling shows the cost of delayed transition, which matters to any council planning a similar change to in-house or commissioned care.
findings.figures: 96.3% private bed occupancy
findings.quote: showing in deficit, Brook Meadows House (BMH), and Reablement.

findings.headline: Southend Care Ltd's draft 2025/26 accounts show a profit of £481.7k, plus a one-off in-year efficiency saving of £424.7k back to Southend-on-Sea City Council.
findings.detail: The paper says the draft 2025/26 statutory accounts were signed off by the company board on 23/09/26. It also says current in-year performance is ahead of budget, and the company will seek to improve on the budgeted profit for the current year.
findings.matters: A council-owned company returning a one-off saving to the council's general budget is a direct cash effect on the council's position, and finance officers elsewhere may be weighing similar arrangements.
findings.figures: £481.7k profit; £424.7k one-off in-year efficiency saving
findings.quote: show a profit of £481.7k, in addition to a one off in-year efficiency saving of £424.7k back to SCC.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Decision Report Unit4 Contract Variation
findings.headline: Southend-on-Sea proposes to fund a £2,800 a year (ex VAT) Unit4 ERP licence variation from its existing approved capital budget.
findings.detail: The report states that the recurring annual cost of the SSMS access will be met from capital rather than revenue. It also says the proposal does not generate a direct cashable saving and is not intended to reduce expenditure within the Medium-Term Financial Strategy.
findings.matters: A recurring annual software cost charged to a capital budget is a treatment a finance director, or a peer council checking its own capital and revenue boundary, would want to look at.
findings.figures: £2,800 ex VAT per annum; 0.28% of the overall Unit4 contract value; original contract up to 36 months at £1,007,934.33 plus VAT
findings.quote: The additional annual cost of £2,800 ex VAT will be met from within the existing approved capital budget.

findings.headline: The council has progressed procurement of TPPL fleet services, with a phased move to newer vehicles.
findings.detail: Following scrutiny of an individual cabinet member decision by the Policy & Resources Committee on 8 October, the council has progressed the procurement in line with the agreed recommendations. The paper says the procurement is intended to secure a compliant and sustainable transport solution and support fleet modernisation.
findings.matters: Fleet replacement is a capital commitment for a transport operator, and other councils facing similar SEND-driven capacity needs may be considering the same choice between buying and contracting.
findings.quote: the Council has now progressed the procurement of TPPL fleet services in line with the agreed recommendations

findings.headline: The paper estimates that delivering routes through Vecteo's directly managed fleet rather than external contractors saves around £287,000 a year.
findings.detail: The original business case put routes costing approximately £843,000 through external contractors at approximately £556,000 when delivered by Vecteo. The paper says demand growth has made the financial benefit of in-housing more significant.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing in-house and contracted SEND transport can use this as a worked example of the cost difference, though it is the council's own estimate from the original business case.
findings.figures: £843,000 external contractor cost; £556,000 Vecteo cost; £287,000 full year savings
findings.quote: generating full year savings of around £287,000

findings.headline: SEND passenger numbers have risen by 73 children and young people since Vecteo's budget assumptions were developed, and an additional £150,000 was added to the original budget.
findings.detail: The paper says the council and Vecteo could not fully anticipate the scale of growth in SEND transport demand. The added pressure led to additional route requirements and vehicle resource pressures, which the paper says were resolved by procuring a newer fleet. The Board approved the adjusted budget in May 2026.
findings.matters: Growth in SEND transport demand is a pressure on council transport budgets that finance officers at other authorities are likely to be tracking.
findings.figures: 73 children and young people; £150,000 additional budget
findings.quote: has increased by 73 children and young people

findings.headline: Vecteo's 2026/27 budget forecasts income of £5,563,000 and a surplus of £202,000, depending on the business plan and decisions on returning savings to SCC.
findings.detail: The paper states the budget generates income of £5,563,000 and a surplus of £202,000, with the surplus dependent on the success of the business plan and on decisions about returning savings to the council. A reserves policy for Vecteo is due for consideration at a forthcoming Board meeting.
findings.matters: A council trading company whose surplus depends on in-housing savings and on decisions about returning money to the parent council is a structure other finance directors may be weighing for their own transport services.
findings.figures: £5,563,000 income; £202,000 surplus

findings.paper_title: Final Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 and Statement of Accounts 2025-26 - covering report
findings.headline: Southend-on-Sea published audited 2024-25 accounts on 13 January 2026, 45 days ahead of the 27 February 2026 statutory deadline, recovering from being 566 days late in 2020-21.
findings.detail: The council's audit completion has improved dramatically. 2020-21 accounts published 19 April 2023 against 30 September 2021 deadline (566 days late); 2021-22 published 19 December 2023 against 30 November 2022 (384 days late); 2022-23 published 28 November 2024 against 30 September 2023 (421 days late). 2024-25 was published 45 days early. The paper states 2025-26 is expected to publish 'well in advance of the statutory backstop date of 31 January 2027', indicating the turnaround continues.
findings.matters: A council publishing 566 days late signals severe finance function distress; recovery to 45 days early signals materially improved financial management capability, relevant to peer councils managing audit backlogs and to lenders assessing financial governance strength.
findings.quote: On 13 January 2026 the signed and audited Statement of Accounts for 2024/25 were published, thereby meeting the statutory backstop date for that financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - KPMG Auditors Annual Report for year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing identified serious failings in September 2025 (C3 rating); fire, electrical and gas safety compliance improved to 98% by March 2026
findings.detail: The Regulator for Social Housing conducted an onsite inspection in April 2025 and issued a C3 rating on 24 September 2025, concluding there are serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of consumer standards and significant improvement is needed. The council responded with a consumer standards improvement plan and active engagement with the regulator. By March 2026, fire, electrical and gas safety compliance had improved significantly to approximately 98%, a substantial increase from April 2025 baseline. The auditor concluded the council has an appropriately robust response with effective monitoring through governance committees.
findings.matters: This indicates significant compliance and governance issues in housing management for a council owning approximately 6,000 homes. However, it also demonstrates the council is responding effectively with tangible improvements, indicating manageable rather than intractable governance risk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - KPMG Auditors Annual Report for year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Greater Essex local government reorganisation paused on 7 September 2026; April 2028 implementation now subject to government review with updates expected Summer 2027
findings.detail: The council developed and secured government approval in March 2026 for reorganisation into 5 unitary councils combining Southend, Castle Point and Rochford, originally planned for April 2028. On 7 September 2026, the government announced a review of the entire local government reorganisation programme and paused the process. The timetable and scope are now subject to further government decisions. While the LGR work created significant resource demands during 2025-26, the auditor found no indication of deterioration in business-as-usual operations.
findings.matters: A major structural change to the council was approved and planned, creating investment and resource commitments. The pause creates planning uncertainty for the council and its lenders regarding governance structure, service delivery models, and potential transition costs.
findings.figures: 5 unitary councils proposed (replacing 15 councils); implementation date April 2028 (now paused); updates expected Summer 2027
findings.quote: On 7 September 2026, the Government announced a review of the local government reorganisation programme following updated legal advice. findings.paper_title: Appendix - KPMG Auditors Annual Report for year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £5.5m in 2025-26 with forecast £7.1m overspend in 2026-27 P4
findings.detail: Social Care and Healthier Communities directorate reported a £5.5m adverse variance against a revised budget of £60.7m in 2025-26 (revised from initial £47.8m). The overspend was driven by activity numbers and care package costs rising above inflationary assumptions, with demand significantly exceeding prior year levels. The directorate also incurred £1.26m in unforeseen costs when a direct payment provider went into administration. P4 2026-27 forecasts a continuing £7.1m overspend.
findings.matters: This is a separate but concurrent structural overspend to Children's Services. Two major demand-led service areas overspending simultaneously and forecast to continue indicates sector-wide cost pressures the council cannot absorb through existing budget assumptions.
findings.figures: £5.5m overspend 2025-26; revised budget £60.7m (from initial £47.8m); £1.26m from provider failure; £7.1m forecast overspend 2026-27 P4 against revised budget £67.2m

findings.headline: Usable reserves fell £16.8m to £166.0m with £25.1m transferred from earmarked reserves to cover General Fund overspend

This represents significant depletion of resources held to manage financial uncertainty, particularly concerning given the forecast continuation of the underlying overspends in social care services.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion indicates financial sustainability risk. A council using earmarked reserves to offset structural operational overspends is on a concerning trajectory, especially when the underlying pressures in children's and adult services are forecast to continue.
findings.figures: Usable reserves £166.0m (down from £182.9m); £25.1m transferred from earmarked reserves; General Fund overspend £12.0m; target minimum unallocated reserves £8.0m annually through 2030-31

findings.paper_title: Appendix - KPMG Auditors Annual Report for year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Children's Services overspend widened to £11.6m in 2025-26, up from £6.1m in 2024-25, with forecast continuing at £5.58m in 2026-27 P4
findings.detail: The Children, Young People and SEND directorate reported a £11.6m adverse variance against its revised budget of £54.5m in 2025-26, with total expenditure increasing from £55.6m to £66.1m year-on-year. Although the Council avoided approximately £4m in additional costs through intervention, P4 2026-27 forecasts a continuing £5.58m overspend against a revised budget of £56.76m.
findings.matters: A lender must distinguish between one-off and structural overspends. This is recurring across multiple years and forecast to continue despite increased budgets and management intervention, indicating a structural issue in social care demand the council cannot absorb.
findings.figures: £11.6m overspend 2025-26; £6.1m overspend 2024-25; total expenditure £55.6m (2024-25) to £66.1m (2025-26); £5.58m forecast overspend 2026-27 P4 against revised budget £56.76m
findings.quote: The outturn reported an adverse variance of £11.6m.

findings.headline: Post-close adjustments totalling £32m expenditure and £24.6m income processed outside core financial system and subject to manual controls
findings.detail: A significant number of post-close adjustments required to produce statutory accounts were identified as processed outside the core financial system and instead maintained manually across 35 spreadsheet columns for expenditure (£32m) and 24 spreadsheet columns for income (£24.6m). Although management review procedures are in place, these adjustments are not subject to system-based controls or automated validations. The council is exploring implementation of a Financial Planning and Analysis module to address this, with procurement expected in October 2026 and implementation targeted for 2027/28. In the interim, enhanced senior officer review has been put in place for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Material adjustments outside the core financial system increase the risk of undetected error, create audit inefficiency, and indicate that the council's financial systems may not be fit for statutory accounting purposes.
findings.figures: £32m expenditure across 35 spreadsheet columns. £24.6m income across 24 spreadsheet columns.
findings.quote: A significant number of post-close adjustments were identified through the Income & Expenditure (I&E) portfolio workings, which were processed outside the core financial system. These adjustments—totalling £32 million in Expenditure across 35 spreadsheet columns, and £24.6 million in Income across 24 spreadsheet columns—were manually maintained and not subject to system-based controls or automated validations.

findings.headline: Management review control over valuation identified as ineffective; recommendation to enhance sampling of property grouping and data checking in next full revaluation in 2030
findings.detail: KPMG found that whilst management performed a review of the year-end Council Dwelling valuation, the control was ineffective because auditors identified errors that management's review had not caught. These included instances where the valuer had inadvertently changed the data used in valuations and assigned incorrect values to properties. KPMG has recommended that for the next full revaluation in 2030, management increase their review to include checking property grouping includes only similar properties and comparing valuation spreadsheet data to council records. The council accepted this and will implement on a sample basis for the 2030 revaluation.
findings.matters: Ineffective management review controls over material asset valuations indicate internal control weaknesses that increase audit risk and the likelihood of undetected errors; councils relying on ineffective controls create financial reporting risk.
findings.figures: Review testing of sample of 68% of council dwellings identified variations requiring challenge to valuer. 5 properties identified as inappropriately grouped.
findings.quote: we have identified several areas where the valuer had inadvertently changed the data used in valuing the properties, and instances where the valuer had assigned a property an incorrect value

findings.detail: KPMG has identified one significant risk in the Council's arrangements to secure value for money in the financial sustainability domain. This is distinct from the governance and economy/efficiency domains, where no significant risks were identified.
findings.matters: Councils are required to demonstrate value for money in use of resources; a significant risk in financial sustainability can lead to a qualified value-for-money opinion and signals to lenders that the council may face budget or financial management challenges.

findings.quote: We have identified 1 risk of a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements to secure value for money. To date we have not identified any indicators to suggest a significant weakness exist.

findings.headline: Investment portfolio reduced by £25.6m following maturity and non-reinvestment of £25m fixed-term deposits
findings.detail: The council's investments fell from £77.3m at 31 March 2025 to £51.6m at 31 March 2026. The material movement was due to £25m of fixed-term deposits maturing in the period and not being reinvested. The remaining movement of approximately £0.7m reflects valuation changes on property and bond funds. This represents a significant change in the council's liquid asset position and investment strategy.
findings.matters: Councils managing a £25m reduction in investment holdings signals a change in liquidity or investment approach; lenders track councils' working capital positions and investment choices.
findings.figures: Investments £77.3m (31 March 2025) down to £51.6m (31 March 2026). Fixed-term deposits matured £25m. Other valuation movement c.£0.7m.
findings.quote: Investments fell from £77.3m to £51.6m. The drop is due to £25m of fixed term deposits maturing in the period and not being reinvested.

findings.headline: £1.736m uncorrected pension liability misstatement due to disagreement with actuary over asset ceiling calculation
findings.detail: KPMG identified a difference with the council's actuary on how to treat additional funding contributions made by the council in the year. The actuary classified these as secondary deficit contributions and included £1.736m as an additional liability within the asset ceiling restriction. KPMG assessed these contributions as primary in nature and considers that no additional liability should be recognised. This uncorrected misstatement overstates the net pension liability by £1.736m (0.3% of total reserves). The council recognised a net pensions liability of £4.652m after a £307.9m asset ceiling impact.
findings.matters: The valuation of pension liabilities is material to council accounts and reserves; disagreement between the council's advisers and auditors on classification of contributions shows estimation uncertainty and affects whether the reported liability position is accurate.
findings.figures: £1.736m uncorrected misstatement. Net pension liability £4.652m. Asset ceiling impact £307.9m. Funded surplus calculated by actuary: £306.193m.
findings.quote: the actuarial report also included an additional liability of £1.736 million in respect of additional funding contributions made by the Council in year which the actuary have assessed to be secondary deficit funding contributions. Based on our understanding of the Council's funding arrangements this amount does not relate to deficit funding contributions but are instead primary contributions. It is our assessment that no additional liability should be recognised at year end relating to these payments.

findings.headline: Council dwellings valuation control found ineffective; £434.9m asset has residual audit uncertainty over property grouping accuracy
findings.detail: The gross book value of council dwellings fell from £484.5m at 1 April 2025 to £434.9m at 31 March 2026. The auditors have queries outstanding with the valuer on data used for 2 other sampled properties and note that work to determine whether the grouping error could cause a material misstatement remains ongoing.
findings.matters: Councils use property valuations to determine both the balance sheet position and in-year revaluation movements; control failures over a £434m asset class indicate financial reporting risk and affect the auditors' ability to sign the opinion on time.
findings.figures: £434.9m (31 March 2026), down from £484.5m (1 April 2025). Sample testing covered 68% of population.
findings.quote: our audit procedures identified further errors. We have raised a recommendation to address this control finding on page 28

findings.headline: Southend-on-Sea unitary council creation formally stopped after government pause on 7 September 2026
findings.detail: The Government paused its March 2026 minded-to-decision to create five Greater Essex unitary councils, and the plan is now under government review. findings.headline: Waste collection contract pressures of £0.670M from inaccurate original survey data
findings.detail: New waste collection and street cleansing contract operational since April 2025 with wheeled bin transition completed October 2025. Original contract specification (Q4 2023/24) assumed higher numbers of properties could move to wheeled bins based on property data at the time. Current administration commissioned a comprehensive property survey revealing more properties must remain on weekly sack collections than assumed, creating £0.460M estimated pressure. Additional £0.210M pressure on residual waste disposal costs and £0.130M on garden waste income shortfall against forecast.
findings.matters: Contract management risk. The council is locked into a multi-year contract based on incorrect property data assumptions. The council is 'continuing to work' to mitigate, but cost pressures are now crystallising. Garden waste subscription levels also came in below assumption.
findings.figures: £0.460M pressure on weekly sack collections vs. assumed wheeled bin uptake. £0.210M residual waste disposal pressure. £0.130M garden waste income shortfall. Total waste/environment pressure in portfolio: £0.696M.
findings.quote: The original contract specification, developed in Q4 2023/24, assumed a higher number of households would transfer to wheeled bins, based on property information provided at the time. The current administration subsequently commissioned a comprehensive property survey, providing a more accurate assessment of which properties could move to wheeled bins. This identified that more properties would need to remain on weekly sack collections than assumed in the original contract modelling, creating an estimated £0.460M forecast pressure.

To accelerate transformation, council is seeking to adopt a Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy to invest capital resources in programmes that 'reduce ongoing costs, improves services and delivers long-term financial benefits.' £8.0M of eligible capital receipts (from Delaware Campus sale £3.5M plus other receipts) is proposed for transformation expenditure.
findings.matters: The council is missing 20% of its approved savings at Period 4 of a 12-month year. The fact that nothing is rated Red is positive, but Amber-rated items can slip. More concerning: the council is betting on capital-funded transformation to solve a £13-28M recurring cost problem. This strategy requires transformation to deliver; failure is not an option.

findings.headline: Reserves increased to £12M but council acknowledges they cannot fund recurring statutory pressures indefinitely
findings.detail: Council increased General Fund Reserve to £12M, described as 'the highest level it has ever held.' The s151 Officer recommends maintaining this level through 2030/31. However, the paper explicitly states 'Reserves provide financial resilience but cannot fund recurring statutory pressures indefinitely. Any drawdown should be replenished given the challenging funding outlook for 2027/28 and 2028/29.' The 2025/26 outturn showed a £12.0M overspend 'driven principally by demand-led statutory social care pressures. Strong financial management and reserves enabled the Council to manage this position, but continued growth in statutory demand and costs cannot be met through reserves indefinitely.'
findings.matters: Reserves are a financial buffer, not a solution. A council building reserves while facing recurring structural overspends is acknowledging that near-term resilience (£12M buffer) masks a medium-term insolvency if structural pressures are not solved. The paper shows the council drawing £12M from reserves in 2025/26 and forecasting £13.3M overspend in 2026/27 — reserves are being consumed at £12-13M per year while the MTFS shows a £28.5M gap by 2030/31.
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve: £12M (highest ever held). 2025/26 overspend: £12.0M. 2026/27 forecast overspend: £13.291M. Medium-term gap by 2030/31: £28.5M.
findings.quote: Reserves provide financial resilience but cannot fund recurring statutory pressures indefinitely. Any drawdown should be replenished given the challenging funding outlook for 2027/28 and 2028/29.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account overspend of £0.850M driven by repair and maintenance cost increases

The paper states HRA 'remains in a strong financial position overall' but identifies rent collection as an ongoing risk 'amid ongoing economic pressures affecting local tenants.'
findings.matters: Damp, mould and condensation are statutory compliance issues (Housing Regulator judgment noted; ongoing improvement tracking mentioned). They cannot be deferred. Rising repair costs on a fixed rent base suggest either deferred maintenance is being revealed or the stock condition is deteriorating. Rent collection pressure indicates tenant economic stress.

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation increasing 17% despite using own housing stock
findings.detail: Families in temporary accommodation are up 17% in 2026/27. The Council is using its own housing stock wherever possible, but demand exceeds supply, requiring use of more expensive nightly-let and bed-and-breakfast accommodation to meet statutory duties. This is forecast to create a £0.380M overspend. The council is pursuing a £100M multi-year housing investment programme approved in July 2025 to increase affordable housing and reduce TA pressure.
findings.matters: Homelessness is both a demand pressure and a leading indicator of economic stress among residents. A 17% increase in one year suggests economic deterioration in the resident base. It is also a cost pressure growing despite the council's own-stock mitigation strategy.
findings.figures: 17% increase in families in temporary accommodation. Forecast £0.380M overspend on TA costs. £100M multi-year housing investment programme approved to increase affordable housing.
findings.quote: Homelessness demand continues to increase, with 17% more families placed in temporary accommodation in 2026/27. The Council is using its own housing stock wherever possible, but demand continues to exceed supply, requiring the use of more expensive nightly-let and bed and breakfast accommodation to meet our statutory duties.

findings.headline: Supported accommodation creating £2.3M gross pressure in 2026/27 from shift in claimant caseload to people ineligible for subsidy
findings.detail: The Council is experiencing a £2.3M gross financial pressure from supported accommodation, driven by a shift in the claimant caseload towards non-vulnerable people who do not meet Department for Work and Pensions vulnerability criteria. For vulnerable claimants, the Council can claim 60% subsidy; for non-vulnerable claimants, it receives zero subsidy on rent above the rent officer assessment. The paper explicitly states this 'is not just a local issue but is affecting many areas across the UK' and notes 'the LGA are aware of the challenge and networks are sharing their concerns with the Government.'
findings.matters: This is a policy-driven cost transfer from central to local government. It is not a local efficiency problem — the council is following statutory procedures correctly. A lender needs to understand whether this is a temporary dislocation or a permanent reduction in housing benefit subsidy, which would affect every council. This is explicitly a system failure, not a council failure.
findings.figures: £2.3M gross pressure in 2026/27. Client contributions to adult social care fell from 34% to 31% of costs (£1.5M income loss on Older People care alone). Supported accommodation: Council pays actual rent charged by landlord but only claims 60% subsidy if claimant meets DWP vulnerability criteria; for others, no subsidy.
findings.quote: Over the past year there has been a significant increase in the supply of accommodation offering support to clients who do not meet the strict criteria of DWP vulnerability but do still require supported accommodation. The Council has been unable to claim any subsidy reimbursement for benefit paid over the local rent officer assessment in these cases. This is significantly increasing the financial impact and net costs to the Council.

findings.headline: Medium-term budget deficit of £28.5M by 2030/31 with funding growth slowing
findings.detail: The Council approved a Medium-Term Financial Strategy forecasting budget gaps of £9.0M (2027/28), £8.0M (2028/29), £5.8M (2029/30) and £5.7M (2030/31). Government Core Spending Power increases are slowing: 5.1% in 2026/27 down to 3.0% in 2027/28 and 3.4% in 2028/29. The paper explicitly flags this as a risk: 'lower provisional CSP increases forecast for 2027/28 and 2028/29, alongside risks in council tax income assumptions, could place further pressure on the Council's finances.'
findings.matters: A lender assessing a four-year financial horizon faces a council heading towards cumulative deficits it has not yet solved. The council is betting on transformation and service redesign to close these gaps, but has not yet proven this can work at the scale required. The pace of required change accelerates as funding growth slows.
findings.quote: The lower provisional CSP increases forecast for 2027/28 and 2028/29, alongside risks in council tax income assumptions, could place further pressure on the Council's finances.

findings.headline: £13.291M revenue overspend concentrated in statutory social care services

Southend shows both: this is demand-led (more people needing care, more complex needs) and cost-driven (placement market constraints), with the council explicitly noting these pressures cannot be met through reserves indefinitely.

findings.headline: Southend-on-Sea will merge with Castle Point and Rochford to form South East Essex Council from April 2028, following government decision on 25 March 2026.
findings.detail: The Government's Local Government Reorganisation decision will replace the current 15-council system across Greater Essex with five new unitaries. For Southend, this means a structural change effective April 2028. The council is working with the other authorities to develop transition arrangements, and the Greater Essex business case predicts the merger will deliver longer-term efficiencies supported by up-front transitional costs.
findings.matters: For a lender, LGR changes the nature of the borrowing entity and creates implementation risk during 2026-2028; for a finance director, it affects organizational structure, systems, and requires significant transition resources.
findings.figures: £1.5 million allocated to LGR transition costs in 2026/27; merger effective April 2028
findings.quote: The Government's decision on 25 March 2026 to create five new unitary councils for Greater Essex, subject to the necessary Parliamentary approval, will replace the current system of 15 councils. For Southend-on-Sea, this means a new unitary council comprising Southend-on-Sea, Castle Point and Rochford from April 2028.

findings.headline: New waste collection contract is creating £0.460M budget pressure from more properties receiving weekly collection than originally modelled
findings.detail: The waste contract specification was developed in Q4 2023/24. An additional £0.210M pressure exists on residual waste disposal costs.
findings.matters: Unplanned contract cost pressures on a major service suggest inadequate specification or modelling, and point to risk in other major contracts.
findings.figures: £0.460M pressure on weekly sack collection; £0.210M pressure on residual waste disposal costs
findings.quote: There are also more properties receiving a weekly sack collection than was modelled in the original contract specification, developed in Q4 2023/24, which is creating an estimated budget pressure of £0.460M.

findings.headline: 249 properties remain unbanded and unvalued by the Valuation Office Agency, creating Council Tax collection risk and potential bad debt provision
findings.detail: Council Tax base is 115 Band D equivalent properties below budget (61,144.20 actual vs 61,258.91 budget). 249 properties remain awaiting valuation by VOA, with 127 of these from the previous financial year. The council notes that unbanded properties accrue large backdated liabilities that are inherently more difficult to collect than normal instalments, increasing risk of arrears, recovery action, and bad debt provisions.
findings.matters: Collection risk on fundamental council funding source; accumulated backdated liabilities pose higher bad debt risk and indicate potential collection rate deterioration in coming months.
findings.figures: 115 properties below budget Council Tax base; 249 properties awaiting valuation (127 from prior year)
findings.quote: The Council Tax Base as at the end of July 2026 is 61,144.20, around 115 Band D equivalent properties below the budgeted Council Tax Baseline of 61,258.91... At time of writing there are 249 properties awaiting banding, 127 of which were issued in the previous financial year. The longer a property remains unbanded, the greater the balance that accrues before a bill can be issued. Large, backdated liabilities are inherently more difficult to collect than charges spread across normal instalments. This increases the risk of arrears, recovery action, payment arrangements and potential bad debt provisions.

findings.headline: Households presenting as homeless have increased 17%, creating temporary accommodation budget pressures that demand exceeds the council's own housing stock supply
findings.detail: Homelessness demand is surging. The council states demand exceeds supply of its own housing stock, requiring reliance on nightly lets and B&B accommodation. The homelessness service is forecasting £0.325M overspend. The council notes work continues to utilise its own stock where possible, but the scale of need is outpacing internal capacity.
findings.matters: Surge in homelessness demand indicates acute social pressure in the area and creates revenue pressures difficult to control through operational measures, with potential for further deterioration.
findings.figures: 17% increase in households presenting as homeless; homelessness budget overspend £0.325M (£4.942M forecast vs £4.617M budget)
findings.quote: Pressures continue on the temporary accommodation budget, primarily driven by a 17% increase in the number of households presenting as homeless this year. Work continues to try and utilise our own housing stock where possible but demand exceeds supply and as a result nightly lets and B&B accommodation is also required.

findings.headline: Universal Credit rollout and shifts in benefit claimant demographics are creating £2.3M gross additional pressure on benefit administration costs
findings.detail: National welfare policy changes and Universal Credit continue to drive higher net costs. The council's benefit claimant caseload has shifted towards supported accommodation. Gross additional pressure is £2.3M; mitigating actions of £0.7M have been identified, leaving net overspend of £1.173M on Council Tax, Business Rates and Benefits. This is a pressure outside the council's control.
findings.matters: Structural cost pressures from national welfare policy create external dependency; the council manages circa £30M annual Rent Allowances and Rent Rebates but cannot control the policy drivers of cost.
findings.figures: £2.3M gross additional pressure; £0.7M mitigations identified; £1.173M net overspend in Finance and Transport portfolio
findings.quote: A combination of national welfare policy changes, including the continued rollout of Universal Credit, together with a significant shift in the Council's benefit claimant caseload towards supported accommodation is increasing the net cost to the Council of the circa £30M annual Rent Allowances and Rent Rebates that we administer. The current extra gross financial pressure in 2026/27 is estimated to be circa £2.300M.

findings.headline: Total reserves are forecast to decline from £70.3M (2025/26) to £42.7M (2026/27) and remain at that depressed level through 2030/31
findings.detail: General Fund Reserve is at minimum threshold (£12M). Capital Reserves fall from £4.7M to £3.4M; Corporate Reserves from £13.3M to £4.5M; Grant Reserves from £13.9M to £7.4M; Technical Reserves from £11.5M to £4.7M. This 40% decline and flat line thereafter leaves minimal buffer for unexpected pressures or shocks.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves and no recovery planned through the forecast period limit the council's ability to absorb service pressures or economic shocks, a significant credit weakness.
findings.figures: Reserves 2023/24 £88.1M, 2024/25 £84.4M, 2025/26 £70.3M, 2026/27 onwards £42.7M constant; General Fund Reserve held at minimum £12M
findings.quote: The Council usually maintains it's General Fund Reserve between £10M and £12M in line with the Medium Term Financial Strategy. Given the financial pressures experienced it has been set at £12M for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Cash balances are being deliberately depleted to delay external borrowing, but revenue overspending is accelerating depletion and creating investment income pressure
findings.detail: The council reports £0.4M investment income pressure from deliberately reducing cash balances to defer borrowing. The combination of this deliberate drawdown and reported revenue overspend is accelerating cash depletion, with significant uncertainty about future cash flows. A £0.25M mitigation is assumed if overspends are addressed, but that assumption is not tracking with current delivery.
findings.matters: Accelerating cash depletion combined with persistent revenue overspends creates mounting external borrowing risk and borrowing cost exposure, and indicates the council is running against a hard constraint.
findings.figures: £0.4M investment income pressure; £0.25M assumed mitigation tied to addressing overspends
findings.quote: Cash balances are being deliberately reduced to delay the need for external borrowing, resulting in lower levels of cash available for investment and, consequently, reduced investment returns. Significant uncertainty remains regarding both the timing and value of future cash inflows and outflows. This uncertainty is further compounded by the revenue overspend reported to date against approved budget levels, which is accelerating the depletion of cash balances.

findings.headline: Adult and Children's social care are overspending by £11.5M combined, driven by demand-side pressures the council cannot control
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is forecasting £5.9M overspend: £3.5M from Older People services (increased demand, reduced means-test contributions), £1.9M from physical/sensory impairment services (8% more service users, 21% cost rises). Children's Services is £5.6M over (high-cost supported accommodation, external foster care). Mental Health adds £1.8M pressure. These are structural demand-driven overspends being partially mitigated by scrutiny of placements and vacancies held elsewhere.
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends in statutory services indicate service model sustainability risk and structural inability to contain costs, a material credit concern for lenders.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care £5.872M overspend (£59.070M forecast vs £53.198M budget); Children's Services £5.539M overspend (£46.616M vs £41.077M); Mental Health £1.827M overspend (£9.358M vs £7.531M)
findings.quote: The following pressures are reported within Adult Social Care services: £0.8M Learning Disabilities arising from children transitioning into adult social care this financial year; £3.5M Older People arising from increased demand and costs combined with less contributions from means tested contributions; £1.9M on physical or sensory impairment care packages, this is a result of an increase in service users (+8%) and a general rise in costs (+21%).

findings.committee: Policy and Resources Overview & Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecast overspend of £0.85M driven by additional repairs and maintenance investment of circa £1M

The paper notes 'The performance of the repairs and maintenance contract remains under robust scrutiny. An action plan is described as 'under development'.
findings.matters: The HRA overspend reflects asset condition issues (damp, mould, condensation) that suggest deferred maintenance or quality issues in the housing stock. This creates revenue pressure and potential regulatory risk. The Housing Regulator has previously flagged 'C3 judgement' concerns, which the paper notes the council is responding to. Increasing maintenance costs indicate the housing assets may be deteriorating faster than anticipated.
